theory.overview: Type systems are the backbone of modern programming languages, providing a formal framework for classifying values and preventing errors before runtime. Static type checking catches bugs at compile time, while dynamic typing offers flexibility. Understanding type theory helps you appreciate how languages ensure correctness and enable powerful features like generics and type inference.

sections.title: Static vs Dynamic Typing
sections.content: Static typing (Java, C++, Rust) checks types at compile time, catching errors early. Dynamic typing (Python, JavaScript) checks at runtime, offering more flexibility but potentially more runtime errors.
keyPoints: Static types checked at compile time

sections.title: Type Inference
sections.content: Modern compilers can deduce types without explicit annotations. Languages like Haskell and Rust use sophisticated algorithms (Hindley-Milner) to infer the most general type for expressions.

examples.explanation: Compiler infers x is Int from literal

sections.title: Polymorphism
sections.content: Parametric polymorphism (generics) allows code to work with any type. Ad-hoc polymorphism (overloading) provides different implementations for different types. Subtype polymorphism enables inheritance-based substitution.

keyConcepts.name: Unification
keyConcepts.description: Solving type constraints to find consistent type assignments

steps.title: Type Checking Fundamentals
steps.content: Learn how type checkers traverse AST nodes, maintaining an environment mapping variables to types. Each expression is checked against expected types, building up constraints.

steps.title: Type Constraints & Unification
steps.content: Type inference generates constraints (e.g., 'a must equal int'). Unification solves these constraints by finding substitutions that make all equations consistent.

steps.title: Generic Types
steps.content: Polymorphic types use type variables (like T) that can be instantiated with concrete types. The type checker ensures generic code is used consistently.

practiceProblems.title: Type Inference
practiceProblems.description: Given 'let f = x => x + 1', what is f's most general type?
practiceProblems.solution: int -> int. The + 1 constrains x to be numeric, and the return type matches.

practiceProblems.title: Unification
practiceProblems.solution: T1 = List(Int), T2 = Int. Substitute T2 into first equation.
